learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about RMSNorm's compute pattern from common overgeneralizations.
stem: Select all correct statements about RMSNorm y = x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g. (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: RMSNorm is memory-bandwidth bound in practice: for a row of length N, the kernel reads N x-values and 1 weight tensor once, writes N y-values once, and performs O(N) elementwise operations plus one reduction — the reduction and rsqrt are negligible relative to HBM traffic on modern hardware.
RMSNorm requires a single reduction (E[x^2]) over the normalization axis and no mean subtraction; per-element compute is fewer ops than LayerNorm.
RMSNorm is compute-bound on modern GPUs because the rsqrt and elementwise scaling per element are expensive relative to the memory bandwidth used.
RMSNorm is mathematically identical to LayerNorm applied to zero-mean inputs, so it can always be replaced by LayerNorm with the same weights without changing the trained model.

explanation: A is correct: RMSNorm needs only one reduction (sum of x^2), skipping the mean subtraction and bias of LayerNorm. D is correct: like LayerNorm, RMSNorm is memory-bandwidth bound — HBM traffic (read x, read g, write y) dominates the small per-element compute. B is wrong: 1 flop/byte order-of-magnitude intensity puts it below any modern GPU ridge point. C is wrong: RMSNorm is not just LayerNorm on zero-mean inputs; even in exact arithmetic RMSNorm normalizes by RMS (including the mean^2 contribution), and it has no bias term.

optionExplanations.B: Correct: single reduction; no mean subtraction.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: intensity is O(1) flop/byte — memory bound.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: RMS(x) != sigma(x) even when mean(x) = 0 unless x is zero-mean AND biases match.

assumptions: Weight g is per-feature (one scalar per feature dim).
nonImplications: Does not imply RMSNorm is equivalent to LayerNorm in trained-model semantics.
Does not imply that RMSNorm and LayerNorm produce identical gradients.
